tldr: We propose a framework that uses a video diffusion model to imagine unobserved surrounding future scenes from a single RGB image and an instruction, geometrically aligns SLAM with dense depth predictions to reconstruct a plausible 3D space, and allows a robot to plan safe paths before actually moving.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of HorizonNav. A VLM builds exploration instructions from a single image, and a video diffusion model (Wan 2.2) generates virtual camera videos. From this video, ORB-SLAM3 and Video Depth Anything are coordinated to reconstruct a geometrically aligned 3D point cloud, where an RRT planner independently searches for a safe navigation path for the robot.
overview:
When an autonomous robot navigates unknown environments, conventional SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) treats regions outside the camera's field of view as unknown until the robot physically moves there and points its sensors. If a robot could imagine hidden spots or spaces deep in the scene with high plausibility before moving, it could make optimal path choices much earlier. Recently, video diffusion models that predict future scenes from an image have drawn attention. However, generated videos only look smooth temporally. Their multi-view geometric consistency often breaks down, and the generated camera trajectories themselves can collide into walls, making them unsafe to directly follow for robot motion planning.

To tackle this, the authors developed HorizonNav, a framework that treats the video generation model not as a path to follow directly, but as virtual sensing to lift a geometrically sound 3D space from generated videos. Given a single RGB image and a task instruction, a vision-language model (VLM) creates a virtual exploration instruction, and a diffusion model synthesizes video looking around the environment. Monocular ORB-SLAM3 tracks camera poses and sparse landmarks from this video, while Video Depth Anything's dense relative depth is aligned with the sparse geometric scaffold to reconstruct a consistent 3D point cloud and occupancy grid map. Furthermore, rather than blindly trusting the generated camera motion, an independent sampling-based path planner (RRT) runs over the reconstructed space to derive safe routes.

Experiments confirmed that generating longer video frames with more viewpoints improves planning feasibility (successful path generation in 15 out of 19 scenes). In cases where the generated camera trajectory collides with obstacles, the independent RRT planner recovers safe alternative routes in over 80% of them. Comparisons with LiDAR reference data and real quadrotor flight experiments further demonstrate that imagined 3D maps derived from generated videos are viable for anticipatory path planning.
contributions: Establishing an architecture that treats video diffusion outputs not as direct control trajectories, but as virtual sensor inputs for SLAM and depth estimation, separating path planning from video generation

Proposing a geometry-guided depth alignment method that integrates sparse monocular ORB-SLAM3 landmarks with Video Depth Anything relative depth via robust estimation and edge-preserving filtering to ensure multi-view consistency

Providing quantitative evaluations on the relationship between generated video length (number of viewpoints) and planning feasibility, as well as RRT's ability to avoid collisions present in the generated camera trajectory itself
Performing quantitative geometric diagnostics against external LiDAR data and demonstrating real-world autonomous quadrotor gate passage flights using paths planned in the imagined space

sections.heading: Imagining the Unseen and Planning with Cautious Geometry
sections.summary: Exploring unknown environments benefits from hypothesizing surrounding spaces before a robot moves, but blindly trusting generative models is risky. This paper proposes HorizonNav, which uses video generation as a virtual camera, constructs a safe 3D hypothesis map using SLAM and geometric constraints, and plans paths.
sections.details:
When deploying autonomous mobile robots in unknown environments, conventional visual SLAM can only map regions that have already been observed. Because areas outside the field of view are treated as completely unknown, making efficient, proactive route choices around corners or through doorways is difficult. If a robot could formulate plausible hypotheses about the surrounding space before moving, it could evaluate candidate paths ahead of time. However, such hypotheses must be handled with geometric caution and never overtrusted as ground truth.

Recently, world models using video diffusion to predict future scenes conditioned on robot actions have been actively studied. However, the camera trajectories produced by generative models do not necessarily avoid physical collisions, and generated frames often contain distortions or occlusion inconsistencies that break free-space connectivity. Furthermore, while recent video depth estimation models offer temporal smoothness, they alone cannot guarantee contradiction-free 3D multi-view geometry.

To address this, the authors propose HorizonNav. Guided by a vision-language model (VLM), it drives a video generation model (Wan 2.2) from a single RGB image and language prompt to synthesize virtual camera motion videos. Monocular ORB-SLAM3 then recovers camera trajectories and sparse 3D landmarks, geometrically aligning dense relative depth maps from Video Depth Anything. Finally, an RRT (Rapidly-exploring Random Tree) searches the obstacle space independently of the generated camera trajectory.

A key design philosophy here is clearly separating and validating three questions that are often conflated: whether generated video contains sufficient features for multi-view reconstruction, whether the resulting spatial hypothesis supports downstream path planning, and whether that plan is executable on a physical robot.

sections.heading: Where Generative World Models Meet 3D Reconstruction
sections.summary: We review related work on video prediction for robot action decisions and 3D reconstruction from generated imagery. HorizonNav occupies a distinct niche by keeping the generative model frozen and emphasizing the independence of multi-view geometry and path planning.
sections.details:
Related work is divided into three main categories.

### II-A Generative Future Prediction for Robot Planning
Efforts to leverage predictive imagery for robot decision-making (e.g., Navigation World Models, ImagiNav, NavDreamer) are advancing rapidly. Models that account for multimodal futures and uncertainty have also emerged. However, many prior approaches tie final action decisions directly to trajectories in the generated video or learned latent spaces. In contrast, HorizonNav treats generated video strictly as visual imagination—a virtual sensor—to recover a plausible 3D representation of the surroundings, deriving motion plans independently from that geometric representation.

### II-B Geometric Reconstruction from Generated Observations
Studies combine generative models with explicit 3D structures (e.g., Dream-SLAM, WorldMAP, WonderWorld), and methods like DUSt3R and Depth Anything 3 estimate multi-view geometry directly from images. Other techniques use non-rigid alignment to absorb inconsistencies in generated video. HorizonNav, however, keeps the underlying generative model untouched and directly asks whether commercial off-the-shelf video diffusion models provide sufficient multi-view geometric cues to support robot planning.

### II-C 3D Reconstruction and Navigation Planning
Monocular and video depth estimation models (such as Video Depth Anything) offer high-quality distance cues, but temporal smoothness does not imply geometric correctness. HorizonNav employs time-tested ORB-SLAM3 as a sparse geometric scaffold, constraining dense depth to this skeleton. Considering geometric uncertainties and narrow passages, it adopts sampling-based RRT rather than calculus-based optimization for path search.

sections.heading: How to Build a Reliable 3D Map from Video
sections.summary: We explain the detailed math and mechanisms behind generating exploration prompts with a VLM, synthesizing virtual observations with a video diffusion model, geometrically integrating ORB-SLAM3 and Video Depth Anything into point cloud maps, and planning paths with RRT.
sections.details:
The system consists of three main modules.

First, from the initial image $I_{\mathrm{input}}$ and user task instruction $C_{\mathrm{task}}$, a VLM (Gemini 2.5 Flash) analyzes objects, openings, and unobserved regions. It differentiates visually confirmed areas from uncertain ones and constructs a structured prompt $C_{\mathrm{explore}}$ with anti-hallucination guidance. Based on this, the video diffusion model Wan 2.2 I2V Fast synthesizes a virtual camera motion video, such as moving forward or rounding an opening.

### III-A Trajectory-Guided Relative Depth and Sparse SLAM Landmark Alignment
Across the generated video sequence, monocular ORB-SLAM3 estimates camera poses $\mathbf{T}_{cw}^{t}$ and triangulated sparse landmarks $\mathcal{M}=\{\mathbf{P}_{j}^{w}\}$. Concurrently, Video Depth Anything predicts dense relative depth maps $\hat{D}_{t}$ for each frame. Because these depth maps lack calibrated scale and shift, they are calibrated using the SLAM landmarks as anchors.

### III-A 1 Robust Scale and Shift Estimation
At each frame $t$, the relationship between the camera-frame depth $z_{j,t}$ of SLAM landmarks and the relative depth $\hat{D}_{t}$ is modeled as an affine transformation $D_{t}^{\mathrm{scaled}} = \alpha_{t} \hat{D}_{t} + \beta_{t}$. To suppress outlier effects, an optimization problem combining Huber loss $\rho(\cdot)$ with inter-frame temporal regularization is solved to robustly estimate scale $\alpha_{t}$ and shift $\beta_{t}$.

### III-A 2 Local Residual Correction
Because a global affine transformation leaves local distortions, the residual $r_{j,t} = z_{j,t} - D_{t}^{\mathrm{scaled}}(\pi(\mathbf{K}\mathbf{P}_{j}^{c,t}))$ is computed at each landmark. This residual is propagated to surrounding pixels using a bilateral-like, edge-preserving filter keyed to image intensity changes. This locally corrects the dense depth map while preserving object boundaries and depth discontinuities.

### III-A 3 Dense Point Cloud Reconstruction and Integration
Each corrected depth pixel is unprojected into 3D and integrated into the world coordinate frame using the inverted camera poses from ORB-SLAM3. Downsampling via a voxel grid filter yields a unified point cloud $\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{3D}}$.

### III-B RRT Path Planning in Reconstructed 3D Space
The resulting point cloud is converted into an occupancy grid, inflating obstacles by the robot radius and a safety margin to define the free space $\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{free}}$. Because the imagined space may contain shape distortions and imperfections, gradient-free RRT (Rapidly-exploring Random Tree) is used to find collision-free paths. It is readily applicable to both ground robots (2D pose) and UAVs such as drones (3D position), quickly finding conservative and safe trajectories.

sections.heading: Does Generated Video Actually Help Planning?
sections.summary: We describe four experimental evaluation designs: planning success rates across virtual viewpoint horizons, trajectory independence between generated camera and RRT, external LiDAR geometric diagnostics, and real quadrotor flight tests.
sections.details:
The evaluation centers on a scientific question: can generated virtual viewpoints provide genuine geometric evidence useful for anticipatory robot path planning? Note that feasibility here is defined relative to the reconstructed obstacle representation, not as proof that unknown physical space was perfectly replicated.

### IV-A Planning Utility Across Virtual Viewpoint Horizons
Using prefix lengths of P20 (20 frames), P40, P60, and P81 (81 frames) across 19 scenes, we measure (i) the number of scenes where at least one RRT path was found, and (ii) the RRT success rate across fixed-seed trials. This investigates how extending the horizon to observe farther ahead improves planning feasibility.

### IV-B Virtual Exploration vs. Independent Path Planning
We test the validity of decoupling the robot's path from the generated camera motion. Using two real corridor images (S5, S6), four exploration directions (forward, left, right, enter far right), and two random seeds, 16 videos (32 branched prefix cases) were generated. Projecting the generated camera trajectories onto a common metric obstacle map evaluates whether they violate a 0.20 m collision threshold. If so, we test whether an independent RRT planner can discover a safe alternative.

### IV-C External Geometric Diagnostics
We separate local structural alignment from global metric scale consistency. In a narrow opening (S06 gate scene), traversability is compared between sparse SLAM alone and aligned dense depth (VDA+SLAM). Furthermore, using independently measured Livox LiDAR point clouds as evaluation ground truth, P40 corridor reconstructions are aligned via rigid and similarity transforms (adding a scale parameter) to quantify scale drift and landmark position errors at doorframes and wall corners.

### IV-D Real Quadrotor Flight Validation
To verify whether paths computed in imagined space can be executed in the physical world, six autonomous flight trials with a quadrotor were conducted in a gate-passage setup. Waypoints derived by HorizonNav from a single pre-takeoff image were flown open-loop without online replanning. Motion capture was used solely for state feedback and logging.

sections.heading: Longer Horizons Help, but Dense Depth Has Traps
sections.summary: We report that planning feasibility improves with longer generated videos, RRT recovered alternative paths in 83% of cases where the camera hit walls, mean landmark error against LiDAR was around 0.30 m, and real flight succeeded in 5 out of 6 trials.
sections.details:
Experimental results highlighted both the strengths and unique failure modes of geometric reasoning on generated video.

### V-A Horizon Length and Planning Utility
Across 19 scenes, increasing the frame length from P20 to P81 increased feasible scenes from 13/19 to 15/19, and successful RRT trials rose steadily from 62/90 to 75/90. Extending viewpoints farther forward revealed geometry behind occlusions and openings, helping the planner find valid routes.

### V-B Reconstruction Yield and Failure Pattern Analysis
In a larger archive of 67 generated video cases, ORB-SLAM3 successfully finished 3D reconstruction in 58 cases (yield of 58/67). This confirms feature-based SLAM functions reliably on generated video.
However, among the 58 successful reconstructions, only 36 supported downstream RRT planning, while 22 (37.9%) failed at the planning stage. Failure analyses revealed causes such as virtual camera movements too small to provide sufficient parallax for triangulation, feature tracking drift due to video warping, and hallucinated obstacle bloat in later video frames that sealed off genuinely passable narrow corridors.

### V-C Power of Independent Planning over Generated Trajectories
Out of 25 evaluable corridor cases, the camera trajectory synthesized by the video model violated the 0.20 m obstacle clearance in 6 cases. However, running RRT independently on the reconstructed space successfully found collision-free detour paths in 5 of those 6 cases (83.3%). Even when the generated camera motion collided, the map built from what it saw was accurate enough to find an alternative safe route.

### V-D Quantitative Geometric Diagnostics and Dense Depth Challenges
Aligning 15 corridor cases against LiDAR reference data revealed a mean position error of approximately 0.30 m at structural landmarks like doorframes and corners. Searching for the optimal scale factor yielded a median of 0.995x, close to 1.0x, confirming stable scale calibration.
However, an instructive failure mode surfaced. In the narrow gate passage (S06), sparse ORB-SLAM3 found a feasible crossing path in 5/5 trials, whereas integrating Video Depth Anything's corrected dense depth inflated opening boundaries and blocked the passage completely, preventing path generation (Table IV). This demonstrates that even when dense depth is visually appealing and temporally smooth, it risks creating false obstacles from a traversability standpoint.

sections.heading: How Robotics Should Handle Imagined Spaces
sections.summary: We emphasize that the contribution lies in gaining geometric evidence for planning rather than perfect 3D reconstruction, warn against over-relying on dense depth, and discuss current experimental constraints regarding indoor settings and specific models.
sections.details:
The results support the claim not that video diffusion models perfectly reconstruct unknown physical environments, but the more restrained and realistic claim that generated virtual observations can provide trackable geometric structures useful for anticipatory robot action planning.

The reconstruction yield in the large archive (58/67) shows ORB-SLAM3 can run on generated frames, but as the planning yield (36/58) demonstrates, reconstructibility does not guarantee plannability. Preserving obstacle boundaries and free-space connectivity is what truly matters for robots.

Furthermore, the fact that RRT recovered alternative paths when camera trajectories collided strongly supports decoupling viewpoint motion from the robot's executed path. Conversely, residual errors of ~0.30 m against LiDAR and dense depth closing narrow openings serve as reminders that generated geometry remains purely hypothetical. Safety margins and online validation via physical sensors once the robot begins moving are essential.

While real flight tests achieved 5/6 successful gate crossings, this remains a proof-of-concept in a specific environment. Current limitations include evaluation restricted to indoor spaces, reliance on a single video diffusion model (Wan 2.2), and the lack of a standardized comparison protocol against single-image depth baselines.

sections.heading: Conclusion and Looking Ahead
sections.summary: HorizonNav treats video diffusion models as virtual sensing, building geometrically constrained 3D hypothesis spaces to enable independent anticipatory planning. Future work will explore real-time online validation and deployment across diverse real-world environments.
sections.details:
This paper presented HorizonNav, a framework for anticipatory robot geometric planning from a single RGB image. Wan 2.2 synthesizes hypothetical camera viewpoints, ORB-SLAM3 recovers sparse geometry and aligns metric scale, and an RRT planner uncoupled from the camera trajectory searches the obstacle map.

In 19-scene experiments, extending video length increased plannable scenes from 13 to 15 and RRT trial successes from 62 to 75. The system autonomously recovered alternative paths in over 80% of cases where the camera trajectory collided with obstacles, achieved a mean landmark error of ~0.30 m against LiDAR, and completed 5/6 real quadrotor gate-crossing flights.

In conclusion, while generated virtual imagery cannot be called a complete reconstruction of unknown physical space, it serves effectively as useful geometric evidence for pre-movement planning. Future work includes building fair comparison baselines against single-image depth estimators, conducting generative model and prompt ablations, and developing online validation mechanisms to confirm, refine, or discard imagined maps in real time using physical observations as the robot navigates.

takeaways: Following the raw camera trajectory from a video diffusion model risks colliding into walls, but treating it as virtual sensor imagery for SLAM and running an independent path planner turns it into a powerful tool
Generating longer video horizons with more viewpoints provides richer geometric cues, increasing the success rate of anticipatory path planning

Even visually appealing and temporally coherent dense depth (e.g., Video Depth Anything) can suffer from densification failure modes that seal off openings like doors due to local errors, so it must not be blindly trusted in robotics

When properly calibrated for scale and geometric alignment, 3D spaces lifted from generated video reach structural accuracy around 0.3 m against LiDAR, supporting anticipatory planning and physical drone flights
limitations: Evaluations are limited to indoor environments and rely on a single video diffusion model, Wan 2.2
It cannot fully prevent generative geometric hallucinations, such as hallucinated obstacles expanding late in the video and blocking free space

Flight experiments executed pre-planned paths open-loop before takeoff, without an online validation mechanism to dynamically update or discard imagined maps using new real sensor observations during navigation
